extracted.intended_audience: students of poetry, literary critics, and poets interested in assessing Romantic/Wordsworthian poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the qualities of Wordsworthian/Romantic lyric and narrative poetry — focusing on imagination, diction, pathos, landscape treatment, and formal originality. Useful for critics, students, and poets assessing or emulating this style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meditative pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: A union of deep and subtle thought with sensibility; a sympathy with man as man; the sympathy of a contemplator rather than a fellow-sufferer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic defines 'meditative pathos' as combining subtle intellectual thought and feeling, producing sympathy that contemplates the sameness of human nature across ranks and conditions. Examples cited: poems where calm philosophical feeling and affecting human interest merge (e.g., 'The Affliction of Margaret', 'The Mad Mother').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy of the contemplator
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's sympathy is that of a contemplator (spectator, not particeps): he sees the human face divine even under the dark lines of guilt or calamity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion values an observing, philosophic sympathy that recognizes shared humanity despite social rank, toil, ignorance, or misfortune. The poet's stance is reflective and identifying rather than merely fellow-suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gift of Imagination (highest, strict sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of Imagination in the highest and strictest sense — a faculty that can 'add the gleam' and the 'light that never was' to thoughts and objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination is the supreme creative power (compared favorably to Shakespeare and Milton), responsible for lofty, consecrating, and dream-like poetic effects. The page offers numerous textual examples (e.g., lines from the Yew Trees, Elegiac Stanzas) illustrating this faculty and argues that it pervades much of Wordsworth's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Fancy and Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: A crucial difference: 'in the play of fancy' the poet may be less successful, whereas Imagination is a loftier faculty manifest elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically differentiate passages that are mere 'fancy' (lighter, playful invention) from those exhibiting true Imagination (deep creative synthesis). The text warns that Wordsworth is 'not always' at his best in mere fancy, implying evaluators should identify where higher imaginative power is or isn't operating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent diction that embodies subtle thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A most transparent diction which holds, as in a crystal shrine, a subtle strain of thought and feeling, making the subtle nearly one with the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise clarity and simplicity of language that nevertheless contains and preserves complex thought and feeling. The page cites lines characterized by 'transparent diction' where diction and thought are intimately united and mutually illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of manner (unborrowed kind)
rubrics_metrics.description: A manner or kind 'perfectly unborrowed and his own' — originality even when nearest to great predecessors like Shakespeare and Milton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value originality in voice and treatment: although affinities to canonical figures may exist, the poet's method should remain distinct and self-derived. The critic stresses Wordsworth's unique manner despite comparisons to earlier masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape subordinate to higher human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic landscape is always subordinate to a higher interest (human interest) — landscape serves the moral/psychic/human foreground rather than being an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether nature-painting is used to illuminate human feeling, character, or moral import (e.g., The Wagoner where human figures and Benjamin's story occupy the foreground while landscape encircles them). Where landscape dominates without higher interest, the work is less characteristic of this praised mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonious sweetness and 'Allegro' lightness
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'lightness and spirit — an Allegro touch' in sketches, bringing sweetness and harmonious tone that complements human interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for passages where buoyant, spirited touches enhance the piece's human elements; such 'allegro' qualities should harmonize with rather than undermine depth of feeling (the critic notes this as distinguishing certain sketches from Wordsworth's more solemn work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bold, brief touches in descriptive panorama
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of bold, brief strokes to render striking tracts and produce well-contrasted panoramas of landscape and scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate economy and effectiveness of descriptive lines: short, decisive touches that create a vivid, contrasted panorama (e.g., evening-storm, ale-house interior, dawn on Skiddaw) are praised as masterly strokes of the poetic pencil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to express human passions and affections
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity to represent human passions and affections vividly within poetic composition, even where other great landscape painters fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poet successfully integrates emotional, homely, or lofty human feeling into scenes — e.g., the picture of Benjamin and his temptations, ale-house scenes, and maternal pathos are cited as combining sportiveness with homely pathos effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic pathos in domestic/maternal scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to evoke genuine maternal or domestic pathos with transitions that reveal deranged attention or heightened sensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate passages like 'The Affliction of Margaret' and 'The Mad Mother' for their capacity to move readers: specific stanzas are singled out for their affecting transitions and blended imaginative and passionate power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original treatment of lyric and sonnet forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Sonnets and lyrics that are neither Miltonic, Shakespearean, nor Petrarchan but entirely Wordsworthian and inimitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging formal poems (sonnets, lyrics), look for unique formal voice and manner — originality within traditional forms (examples: sonnets to Sleep, Part I dedicated to Liberty) rather than imitation of established models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of childhood and 'fountain light' vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayal of childhood as a time when 'Heaven lies about us' and the 'fountain light' of early impressions endures as a master light for all seeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value treatments that capture the prelapsarian, visionary aspect of childhood and its lasting influence on perception (quoted passages from the ode about birth, infancy, and the soul). Poems that make childhood's luminous vision a central, sustaining image score highly on this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analogy/allegory to illuminate poetic genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing extended analogies or allegories (e.g., botanical/soil metaphors) as a connected simile to illustrate the poet's intellect and productive capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether analogies and transcribed similes (such as the Bartram 'soil and rock' passage used as allegory) clarify and reinforce judgments about talent and creative potential without becoming merely fanciful ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced simplicity (avoid flattering 'sweet, simple' flattening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic temperament that favors simplicity of subject and diction but resists naive claims of mere sweetness or vulgarity; simplicity should not be mistaken for vacuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should distinguish genuine poetic simplicity (depth under transparent language) from either vulgarity or the affected 'gilded' praise of bland admirers. The page warns against both the detractors who call Wordsworth vulgar and the fawning admirers who reduce him to a 'sweet, simple poet.'
